title: First Aid and Basic Life Support
description: Principles of first aid, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, choking, bleeding, burns, fractures and common emergencies — useful at every level.

topics.title: Principles of First Aid and Scene Assessment
topics.summary: Aims of first aid, scene safety, primary survey (DRSABC) and the recovery position.

notes.b: First aid is the immediate care given to an injured or ill person before professional help arrives. Its aims are the three Ps: preserve life, prevent the condition from worsening, and promote recovery. Always ensure scene safety first — for yourself, bystanders and the casualty — then assess. The primary survey follows DRSABC: Danger, Response (AVPU: Alert, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive), Send for help, Airway, Breathing, Circulation.
k: Three Ps: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery

notes.b: An unresponsive casualty who is breathing normally, with no suspected spinal injury, should be placed in the recovery position (on the side, with the head tilted back and mouth downward) to keep the airway open and allow fluids to drain. Seek consent from conscious casualties; consent is implied for unconscious ones. Use gloves or barriers to reduce infection risk.
k: Recovery position keeps the airway clear

q: The first priority on arriving at an accident scene is:
Ensure the scene is safe before approaching.
In AVPU, 'P' stands for responds to:
Which is NOT one of the three aims of first aid?
Keep the casualty safe from further harm
First aiders do not prescribe drugs; the other options are all part of the three Ps.
An unconscious casualty who is breathing normally, with no spinal injury, should be placed:
Face down with arms under the body
With legs raised and head down
The recovery position protects the airway.
For an unconscious casualty, consent to first aid is:
Not relevant because first aid is illegal
Consent is implied when the casualty cannot respond.
The main purpose of the recovery position is to:
Keep the airway open and let fluids drain
It prevents aspiration of vomit or blood.
Wearing gloves when handling bleeding casualties mainly protects against:
Gloves reduce exposure to HIV, hepatitis B and C.

topics.title: Adult Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR)
topics.summary: Recognising cardiac arrest, high-quality chest compressions, rescue breaths and using an AED.

notes.b: Cardiac arrest is recognised when a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally (gasping, agonal breaths do not count). Call for help and an automated external defibrillator (AED), then start CPR immediately. Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the sternum), the other hand on top, arms straight. Compress 5–6 cm deep at 100–120 per minute, allowing full chest recoil and minimising interruptions.
k: Unresponsive + not breathing normally = start CPR

notes.b: For trained rescuers the ratio is 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, using head-tilt–chin-lift to open the airway; each breath should make the chest rise and last about 1 second. Untrained or unwilling rescuers should give continuous compression-only CPR. Attach an AED as soon as it arrives and follow its voice prompts; ensure nobody touches the patient during analysis and shock. Continue until help takes over, the person shows signs of life, or you are exhausted.
k: Compression-only CPR is acceptable for untrained rescuers
Use an AED as soon as available

q: The recommended compression rate in adult CPR is:
Current guidelines recommend 100–120 compressions per minute.
The recommended compression depth for adults is:
Compress at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm.
The compression-to-ventilation ratio for adult CPR is:
Hand position for adult chest compressions is:
Centre of the chest (lower half of sternum)
Place the heel of the hand on the lower half of the sternum.
Occasional gasping breaths in an unresponsive person should be treated as:
A sign of cardiac arrest — start CPR
Agonal gasps are not normal breathing.
The airway manoeuvre used in an unresponsive adult without neck injury is:
Head-tilt–chin-lift lifts the tongue off the airway.
Analyses rhythm and delivers a shock if needed
AEDs detect shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT) and deliver a shock.
A bystander who is untrained in rescue breaths should:
Hands-only CPR is far better than no CPR.

topics.title: Choking and Airway Emergencies
topics.summary: Recognising and relieving foreign-body airway obstruction in adults, children and infants.

notes.b: Mild obstruction: the person can cough, speak and breathe — encourage coughing. Severe obstruction: the person cannot speak, breathe or cough effectively, may clutch the throat (universal choking sign) and become cyanosed. Act immediately.
k: Severe: cannot speak or cough — act

notes.b: For a conscious adult or child over 1 year with severe obstruction: give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre), alternating. For infants under 1 year: 5 back blows with the infant face-down along your forearm, then 5 chest thrusts with two fingers — never abdominal thrusts. If the casualty becomes unresponsive, lower them to the ground, call for help and start CPR.
k: Adult/child: 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts
Infant: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts

q: A choking adult who can still cough forcefully should be:
Effective coughing is the best way to clear mild obstruction.
Abdominal thrusts are also known as the:
For a choking infant under one year, after back blows you should give:
Infants receive chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts can injure them.
How many back blows are given in each cycle?
Give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 thrusts.
The universal sign of choking is:
If a choking adult becomes unresponsive, you should:
Lower them to the ground and start CPR
Place them in the recovery position and leave
Begin CPR; compressions may dislodge the object.
Blind finger sweeps in the mouth are:
Not recommended; remove only visible objects
Blind sweeps may push the object deeper.
A choking person who cannot speak or breathe has:
Inability to speak or cough indicates severe obstruction.

topics.title: Bleeding, Shock and Wounds
topics.summary: Controlling external bleeding, recognising and managing shock, and basic wound care.

notes.b: Arterial bleeding is bright red and spurting; venous bleeding is dark red and flowing; capillary bleeding oozes. Control severe external bleeding with firm direct pressure on the wound using a clean pad, and elevate the injured limb if no fracture is suspected. If direct pressure fails on a limb with life-threatening bleeding, apply a tourniquet 5–7 cm above the wound and note the time. Do not remove embedded objects; pad around them.
k: Tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding — record time

notes.b: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion. Causes include blood loss (hypovolaemic), severe allergy (anaphylactic), heart failure (cardiogenic) and infection (septic). Signs: pale, cold, clammy skin; rapid weak pulse; rapid shallow breathing; anxiety, confusion and eventually unconsciousness; low blood pressure is a late sign. Lay the casualty down, raise the legs if possible, keep warm, treat the cause, give nothing by mouth and get urgent help. Anaphylaxis requires intramuscular adrenaline (0.5 mg for adults, 1:1000) into the outer thigh.
k: Cold clammy skin, fast weak pulse

q: The first step in controlling severe external bleeding is:
Firm direct pressure controls most external bleeding.
Bright red, spurting blood suggests bleeding from a/an:
Arterial blood is oxygenated and under high pressure.
An embedded knife in a wound should be:
Left in place and padded around
Cut flush with the skin by the first aider
Which is an early sign of hypovolaemic shock?
Rapid weak pulse and cold clammy skin
Compensatory tachycardia and vasoconstriction occur early.
The adult intramuscular dose of adrenaline in anaphylaxis is:
Give 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) IM into the anterolateral thigh.
When applying a tourniquet you must:
Record the time it was applied
Cover it so no one sees
Documenting the time guides hospital management.
A casualty in shock should be given:
They may need surgery or anaesthesia and could vomit.
Low blood pressure in shock is usually a:
The body compensates until significant volume is lost.

topics.title: Burns, Fractures, Seizures and Poisoning
topics.summary: First aid for burns, suspected fractures, seizures, snakebites and poisoning.

notes.b: For thermal burns, cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible, remove jewellery and loose clothing (not stuck clothing), and cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy dressing. Do not apply ice, butter, toothpaste or palm oil, and do not burst blisters. For chemical burns, brush off dry chemicals and irrigate with plenty of water. For suspected fractures, support and immobilise the injured part in the position found, splint above and below the joint, and check circulation beyond the injury. Suspect spinal injury after falls or road crashes and keep the head and neck still.

During a seizure, protect the person from injury, cushion the head, time the seizure and do not restrain them or put anything in the mouth; place in the recovery position afterwards. Call for help if it lasts more than 5 minutes. For snakebite, keep the person calm and still, immobilise the limb, remove rings, and transport urgently to a facility with antivenom — do not cut, suck or apply a tight tourniquet. For poisoning, identify the substance, do not induce vomiting, and seek urgent help (bring the container).
k: Seizure: protect, time, nothing in the mouth
Snakebite: immobilise, no cutting or sucking, antivenom

q: The best first aid for a thermal burn is:
Cool with running water for 20 minutes
Cool running water limits tissue damage and pain.
During a tonic–clonic seizure you should:
Put a spoon in the mouth
Protect from injury and time the seizure
Prevent injury, time it and never put objects in the mouth.
Emergency help is needed if a seizure lasts longer than:
Seizures over 5 minutes risk status epilepticus.
For a snakebite on the leg, you should:
Immobilise the limb and transport to hospital
Immobilisation slows venom spread; antivenom is definitive treatment.
A person who swallowed kerosene should:
Not be made to vomit and be taken to hospital
Vomiting risks aspiration of hydrocarbons into the lungs.
When splinting a fractured forearm, the splint should:
Immobilise the joints above and below
Be very tight to stop swelling
Be applied over the fingers only
Immobilise the joint above and below the fracture.
Clothing stuck to a burn should be:
Removing adherent clothing tears the skin.
After a road crash, a casualty complains of neck pain. You should:
Ask them to turn the head
Keep the head and neck still
Carry them by the arms and legs
Suspect spinal injury and avoid neck movement.
